# Agentic Engineering FaMAF Extension Course

---
created: 2026-03-28
status: draft
tags:

  - agentic-coding

# From Vibe Coding to Agentic Engineering

> 📊 **Presentation** — a plain-language visual walkthrough of this document (the intern framing, the five-level spectrum, LLM + tools + harness, the six weeks, and the model swap): <https://claude.ai/code/artifact/977c4128-625f-42c0-a78d-02e4425a887b>
> Private by default — share it from the page's share menu before sending it to anyone.

Short course for university CS students and Junior programmers with some project experience but little/no professional training. The goal is to walk them through the full spectrum of AI-assisted development — from pure "vibe coding" to structured agentic engineering — building concepts progressively over 6 weeks.

## The Spectrum

1. **Vibe Coding** — pure prompt-and-accept, no code review, iterate only when things break
    1. Vibecoding origin (Karpathy): https://x.com/i/status/1886192184808149383
    2. Vibecoding as videogame (Naval) https://x.com/i/status/2039617101221224858
    3. Kids Vibecoding (usando Lovable): https://www.instagram.com/reels/DKj1ghsiRN3/
    4. Vibe coding in prod (Anthropic): https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fHWFF_pnqDk
2. **AI-Assisted Coding** — copilot-style completions, developer maintains control
3. **Directed AI Assistance** — experienced use of LLMs with constraints, specs, and review
4. **Agentic Coding** — orchestrating AI agents on tasks with oversight
5. **Agentic Engineering** — full discipline: specs, quality gates, multi-agent coordination, accountability
    1. [https://simonwillison.net/guides/agentic-engineering-patterns/](https://simonwillison.net/guides/agentic-engineering-patterns/ )
   

## Key Thesis

Vibe coding is a great on-ramp — fast, fun, empowering. But professional software development demands accountability: security, maintainability, correctness. The course shows *why* each level of structure matters by letting students experience the failures firsthand before introducing the solutions.

**Core mental model: "Managing a smart intern."** The AI is like a capable but inexperienced developer — fast, eager, produces a lot of output, but needs clear direction, regular review, and someone who understands the big picture. You wouldn't accept an intern's code without reading it. You wouldn't let an intern architect your system. The same applies here. This framing recurs throughout the course: each session adds a layer of "management skill" for your AI intern.

## Format

- **6 sessions**, 1 per week, ~2-3 hours each, in two blocks:
  - **Sessions 1 and 5 are the long ones**: Session 1 needs 3 h for introductions plus the install, Session 5 needs 2 h 30 because it opens with an hour of student demos. **Session 2 is the short one, 1 h 30**, the time available for it.
  - **Base — sessions 1-4.** The fundamentals arc: *how do I work well with this thing?* Complete on its own terms, and **Session 4 closes it.**
  - **Advanced — sessions 5-6.** The internals arc: *what is this thing made of, and what if I swap its parts?* **Session 6 closes the course.**
  - **Same cohort throughout** — "advanced" describes depth, not enrollment. Everyone attends all six.
  - **The split is announced to students in Session 1**, on the six-sessions slide, so they know where the base material ends and what changes after it.
  - The shape is not an accident of numbering: the course was originally 4 sessions, and 5-6 were added as a deeper technical arc rather than as more of the same.
- Each session: theory → hands-on → show-and-tell discussion
- **Same project across all 6 sessions** — students see their codebase evolve
- Students bring their own project idea; default fallback is a small web app
- Tool: **Pi** (`pi.dev`) — decided; installed by students in Session 1
- Class size: ~30 students

## Topic Inventory

These are the concepts to cover, roughly ordered by complexity:

### [Diego] Tier 1: Fundamentals
- **Responsibility is the starting point**: accountability stays with the person, not the AI. "The agent wrote it" is not an excuse.
- The AI-assisted coding spectrum (overview)
  - History: https://www.coderabbit.ai/blog/a-very-brief-history-of-ai-coding-from-copilot-to-next-gen-agents
     - 2017: **Paper:  Attention Is All You Need paper introduced the Transformer**, the architecture that made modern large language models possible.
     - 2022: 
       - **(Junio) Github Copilot (Tab Completions)**: Copilot officially becomes generally available to individual developers as a commercial product, standardizing ghost-text style code completions.
       - **(Noviembre) ChatGPT** -- OpenAI releases ChatGPT (GPT-3.5). While built as a general conversational model, developers rapidly adopt it to write, debug, explain code snippets, and scaffold applications via natural language chat.
     - 2023
       - **Cursor:** A dedicated VS Code fork designed from the ground up for LLM integration, deep codebase indexing, and contextual code editing. 
       - **Copilot Chat:** GitHub announces Copilot X, integrating ChatGPT-style sidebar chat and inline conversational editing directly inside the editor.
    - 2024
       - **Cursor Introduces Composer Mode**: Cursor breaks past single-file assistance with the introduction of multi-file reasoning and "Composer", allowing the agent to create and edit entire codebases simultaneously based on high-level instructions.
       - **Windsurf**, a standalone AI-native IDE designed around "Cascade" and agentic flows, emphasizing bidirectional real-time awareness between the developer and the agent across the whole workspace.
    - 2025
      - Anthropic Launches **Claude Code**. Operating primarily as an agentic CLI tool in the terminal, it executes bash commands, searches repositories, edits multiple files, runs tests, and fixes build issues autonomously.
    - 2025 / 2026
      - OpenCode, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, GLM Coding, Kimi CLI, Pi

- Generative AI: what it is, where LLMs sit inside it
- LLM fundamentals: how they work at a practical level — tokens, context windows, probability, why hallucinations happen.
- The model landscape: Anthropic (Claude), OpenAI (GPT), Z.ai (GLM), Moonshot AI (Kimi). Reading a model page: modalities, context window, price. OpenAI's model-comparison page as a way to teach the base concepts in one pass.
- Tokens as the unit of everything: input, output, and price. Multimodality — images and audio become tokens too.
- Pricing shapes: per-token (API) vs subscription, and when each makes sense.
- Context window as finite working memory — and the context rot rule: **try to don't go past 50%** of what the model supports.
- **Context hygiene as operations**, named in the Session 1 hands-on and used from day one: `/session` (tokens and cost so far), `/new` (clean context for an unrelated task), `/compact` (summarize the old part of a long task), `/tree` (rewind to before the agent dug the hole). Four commands, not a topic — the mechanism is Session 5's.
- Chat vs agent: a chat returns text and you execute; an agent executes in a loop (reads, runs, edits, checks, retries).
- Vibe coding: prompt-and-accept workflow. Talk with the agent, don't open files — focus entirely on the output. Working definition: *programar sin pensar que el código existe*.
- Analyzing AI output: what did it actually produce?
- Code quality awareness: dead code? inconsistent patterns? missing tests? mantainability?
- Comprehension debt: you shipped code you don't understand
- Anatomy of a coding agent (brief intro): LLM + tools + harness — just enough vocabulary to use these terms in later sessions
  - Tool: a function the LLM can invoke (read file, run shell, edit code)
  - Coding agent: an LLM that takes actions on a codebase via tools in a loop
  - Harness: the program wrapping the LLM (context management, tool dispatch, permissions). Pi is a harness.
  - The catalogue by environment: web (Lovable, v0, Bolt, Claude Code web), desktop (Claude Code desktop), terminal (Claude Code, Codex, Pi, opencode)


### [Agus] Tier 2: Planning & Review
- AI gets you to something that works, but decisions and details are missing, and you don't know where or how many
- Planning as explore → design → document, then implement from the document. The design can be as light or as thorough as needed; more design costs time up front and buys less rework and more understanding of what comes out
- The design document as a first-class artifact: drafted, read and corrected before it is saved, annotated, versioned, committed with the code. It can carry diagrams, not only prose. `@plannotator/pi-extension` as a small help (*una ayudita*) for annotating it (`/plannotator-annotate`) and the diff (`/plannotator-review`)
- Plan mode (`pi --plan`) as an existing mechanism students can try, not a required step. The harness restricts the toolset to read/search while it is on (seeds Tier 3's permissions/extension-points material)
- Review is getting harder (more code, and code nobody on the team wrote) and the industry is still looking for ways to do it. Two of them used here: moving review earlier, into the design, and verifying that the result works. Reading the diff to understand it and check it against the design
- Testing: the test pyramid (unit, integration, e2e) as vocabulary, and the agent can write all of them. Unattended, you don't know if they test the right thing. Deciding the cases before the code with a simplified Classification Tree Method, each case marked as covered by a test, by the agent's verification, or both
- Verification: the agent exercises what it built. Against an API with `curl`; on screen with a browser-driving CLI (`agent-browser`), introduced in one line since tools are Tier 3's. Verifying becomes the fifth stop after explore → design → document → code
- Debugging AI-generated code: read it yourself before asking for a fix

### [Diego] Tier 3: Tooling & Skills

> Prerequisite, not content: **Pi is installed in Session 1**, and Session 2 adds the Plannotator extension and the `agent-browser` CLI; `pi-subagents` is installed in Session 4, where subagents are taught. Tier 3 goes deeper on the harness — it does not introduce it. `AGENTS.md` **is** introduced here from scratch: the Session 1 step that had students write one was dropped, and Session 2 does not touch it.
>
> **Subagents moved to Tier 4** (decided while building Session 3): Agus opens them there with a documentation use case, so Tier 3 only names them — one row in the always-loaded vs. on-demand table, one row in the extension-points table. Session 2's "depth on subagents is Session 3" promise moves with them.
>
> **Worktrees are out of the course**, not relocated. They were only ever a one-line mention riding along with subagents, no session's hands-on needs them, and Session 2's git block no longer names them either. Cut rather than parked.

- Tools deep dive: what tools are, how the LLM calls them, examples from Pi's toolbelt (read, write, edit, bash, grep, find, ls). Why tools are the unit of capability.
- Harness deep dive: what Pi provides as a harness — context management, tool dispatch, permissions, extension points. Comparison with other harnesses (Claude Code, Cursor, Aider, OpenCode). Why the harness matters as much as the model.
- Custom instructions: `AGENTS.md` from scratch — what it is, the loading order across directories, rules files. Students arrive with the *motivation* for it from Session 2's homework ("what did you have to explain to the agent more than once?"), not with a file.
- Skills / slash commands: teaching AI reusable behaviors. **[Agent Skills](https://agentskills.io/) is an open standard**, not a Pi feature — a folder with a `SKILL.md`, published by Anthropic and adopted across Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot/VS Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, OpenCode and Pi. The three-stage loading taught here is the standard's *progressive disclosure*. Worth one sentence in class: it's the first artefact of the course that transfers to whatever tool the student uses next — and a small rehearsal of what Session 6 makes students verify by hand.
- MCP / external tools: extending the harness — the LLM gains new tools at runtime
- Documentation tools (e.g. [context7](https://context7.com/), [context-hub](https://github.com/andrewyng/context-hub)): fetching up-to-date library docs so the AI works with accurate references instead of guessing
- Subagents: **named only, as the third row of the always-loaded vs. on-demand table** — the work itself can also go to a separate context. The block itself is Tier 4.

### [Agus] Tier 4: Context Engineering
- Problem domain vs. solution domain: the same feature described as a need (actors, data and relations, processes, in problem terms) and as a system (data diagrams, breadboards/page sketches, flows). Starting from the solution means deciding without having considered the problem in depth, and inheriting the agent's average answer for every decision left open.
- Living project documentation as context: `docs/PROJECT.md` (what the project is, main goal, constraints) plus one doc per feature (the problem it solves, then a design section with the model and one flow per interaction — each flow carries its screens, steps, rules and decisions with their reasons). Committed to the repo; `AGENTS.md` points to them.
- Writing docs with the agent: interrogation before drafting — the agent asks, the student decides (e.g. Matt Pocock's grill-me skill). Delegating the writing is fine; delegating the thinking is the failure mode.
- Research feeds the docs at high level: documentation tools (context7) to understand a library, while implementation details belong to the plan, not the doc
- Subagents, the primitive: delegating a subtask to a separate context, and the available agent types (research, exploration, review). Moved here from Tier 3, and **opened through the research above** — sending the library research to its own context is where the delegation pays for itself, so the primitive and its best motivation land together.
- The chain: doc → plan → implementation → review (the review checks against both the plan and the doc)
- Cognitive debt and cognitive surrender: the cost of repeatedly delegating reasoning to the AI, and adopting its decisions as your own opinions
- When to delegate vs. intervene (developing intuition)
- Professional accountability: you sign off on what the AI produces
- Orchestration, in passing: shared docs as the ground truth that lets several agents work in parallel
- Cost and limits: tokens as a budget, model tiering, when NOT to use AI, skill atrophy, and what skills matter in an AI-augmented world. This tier closes the *"how do I work well with this thing?"* arc, so the judgment material lives here. The full-course retrospective belongs to Tier 6. (The spectrum revisit used to as well; it no longer happens anywhere.)

### [Agus] Tier 5: Harness Internals

> **The spine: teach the concept, use Pi as the specimen.** Every topic here is a design decision *any* harness has to make; Pi is the one we can open, not the one being sold. That rehearses Tier 6's model swap a week early. The failure mode of this tier is turning into a tour of Pi's features.

- What a harness is, revisited from Tier 1: interface, agent loop, tools/memory/context, model. An LLM alone predicts tokens and can do nothing; the harness connects it to the world.
- **The other harnesses, as axes rather than a ranking**: open vs. closed source, what ships built in vs. what you add, whether there is an extension surface and how deep it reaches, who controls the system prompt. The questions to ask the next tool they pick up. **No comparison table** — comparing harnesses in the abstract is useless to someone who has used one.
- The agent loop, step by step, with the extension points on the arrows: `session_start`, `resources_discover`, `input`, `before_agent_start`, `turn_start`, `context`, the model call, `tool_call`, `tool_result`, `turn_end`, `agent_end`, `session_shutdown`. Every moment is subscribable, and from there you block, modify or inject. **This is where Tier 2's plan mode finally gets its mechanism**: `tool_call` → `{ block: true }`.
- Harness architecture as layers, and the idea that you use only the ones you need. Pi's four packages: unified model API, generic agent loop, coding layer, terminal UI.
- **Sessions as a tree, not a list**: entries with `id` and `parentId`, the active leaf, the whole tree in one file. Why `/tree` is cheap — you move a pointer, you don't delete. Tier 1 sold it as the antidote to cascading errors; here it gets its reason.
- **Steering vs. follow-up**: when does new information reach an agent that is already running? Interrupt mid-stream, wait for it to settle, or queue for the next turn. Every harness decides this; most hide it.
- **Three ways to give a model a tool**, and the tradeoffs: an **extension** (reaches harness internals, works in that harness only), a **CLI** (simplest, portable to any harness with a shell, no auth story, and the agent has to learn it exists — which is what `AGENTS.md` is for), **MCP** (for tools other people consume: distribution, auth, remote services, paid for in context). The question that decides it is who the consumer is.
- **Subagents, the mechanism** (the use case is Tier 4's): a separate context with its own transcript, whose entire result returns to the parent as one message. The honest reason is context economy, not "more AI".
- **Compaction**, the debt Tier 1 assigned here: the trigger (`contextTokens > contextWindow - reserveTokens`), the algorithm (walk back to `keepRecentTokens`, cut, summarize the older half in a structured format, store the summary with the first kept entry), and the two consequences — it is lossy and it is another model call, and it is interceptable.
- **Run modes**: interactive, headless one-shot, embedded as a library, served behind a protocol. The agent loop is a library and the terminal is one of its interfaces. Why CI agents, bots and in-browser agents exist.
- **Security, generalized**: threat models (prompt injection from repo content, a malicious extension/skill/MCP server, the agent's own destructive mistakes, credential exfiltration), permission models as a design space, and the sandbox ladder (none → in-process → container → micro-VM → separate machine). The counterintuitive argument worth stating: **a partial sandbox is worse than none**, because it reads as a boundary while still resting on your shell, filesystem, package managers and credentials. Real isolation comes from the OS.

### [Diego] Tier 6: Open Source Models & HPC

> 🔴 **TO REVIEW** — Claude-generated, not yet reviewed by Diego.

- **Open source vs. open weights**: open weights means you can download and run them; open source in the strong sense means you could reproduce the model (training code + data information). Nearly everything marketed as "open source AI" is open weights — the binary, not the recipe.
- **Licences**, where that distinction gets consequences: standard software licences (Apache 2.0, MIT) vs. bespoke licences with usage restrictions and scale clauses (Llama community licence, Gemma terms) vs. restrictions on the output itself. The three questions to answer before shipping: commercial use? redistribute a fine-tune? who owns the generations?
- Honest about the capability gap on long-horizon agentic work and reliable tool calling. **The control-spectrum table was cut** when the theory block moved to Copes's arc — the tradeoffs are still named, through his five reasons and his list of what open weights do not guarantee.
- **Is an open model good enough to be the engine of a serious project?** No longer a taught block — 150 minutes do not hold it. It survives as written material in the exercise (Raschka's measurements, and when open source is the right call), and the VRAM figure goes to Agus to close his demo. The line worth keeping wherever it lands: the bottleneck is usually reliable tool calling, not the ability to write code.
- **Running one on your own hardware**, made concrete: **Agus's 15-minute demo** — a portable eGPU on the desk, Ollama on CUDA, and the quantization arithmetic from the theory checked against 16 GB of real VRAM. He shows, the room watches; it is not an endpoint students connect to.
- What it takes to run one: what a download actually gets you (safetensors vs. GGUF, tokenizer, runtime, the token loop), quantization and its cost to structured output — i.e. to tool calling — and the OpenAI-compatible endpoint that lets any harness point anywhere. **The local-vs-serving runtime distinction is no longer taught as a block**; the guest owns batching in his slot, and the contrast has a real referent in the room instead: CCAD runs **vLLM** behind its gateway because it serves many users, while Agus's demo runs **Ollama** on one card.
- **The context window is paid for in VRAM, not just declared.** The best single moment of the theory arc, and it needs the demo to land: `30B × 4 bits ≈ 15 GB` of weights against a 16 GB card reads as "it just fits" and does not, because the KV cache lives there too. It returns twice more — as `--max-model-len` on CCAD's side, and as `contextWindow` in the student's own JSON.
- The OpenAI-compatible endpoint as the interoperability story: why a harness can point at a different model by adding a provider to its config. This is the technical bridge from Tier 5.
- **The inference gateway.** CCAD is reached through a **LiteLLM** proxy exposing an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, and Pi gets there with a provider entry in `~/.pi/agent/models.json` — no SSH, no scheduler, no tunnel. Swapping the model is a config file. Two things that fall out of it and are worth teaching: the context window turns out to be a startup parameter somebody chose (server-side here, chosen by the student with `-c` in the local track), and **a gateway is also a third party** — "runs on UNC hardware" is not the same as "nobody sees my prompts".
- Shared-resource etiquette, in one line when the hands-on is released: people are running their theses on those machines. **Cluster mechanics are out of the course** — login vs. compute node, the scheduler, modules, port forwarding are internals of a multi-user inference service; the guest touches them lightly and that's it.
- **CCAD (Centro de Computación de Alto Desempeño, UNC)**: a 60-minute guest talk by Ale Silva, and the programme is his — an introduction to HPC and why clusters are needed; UNC Supercómputo's history, clusters and metrics, and where it stands against the region and the world; the experience of deploying models on limited hardware and turning a working test into a stable multi-user service; and how to use CCAD's resources, from requesting an account to making a first call to their models. Most students don't know UNC runs an HPC center they can use. **Access is the takeaway that outlives the course** — and it is explicitly the road back *after* the course, not today's access, which runs on a key Diego hands out. His third point is where LiteLLM and vLLM get named by the person who chose them, fifteen minutes before students type them into `models.json`. Cluster mechanics stay out — light touch only.
- Supply chain and self-hosting risk: what you trust when you download multi-gigabyte binary weights; how self-hosting removes a third party and adds you as the operator.
- When open source is the right call: sensitive data, cost-dominated volume, research reproducibility, offline work, studying the model itself — versus wanting the best coding agent today with no ops capacity.

### Cross-cutting: Security & Trust (woven throughout)
Not a dedicated session, but surfaced where relevant:
- **Session 1**: security issues found during code analysis (common vulnerabilities in AI output)
- **Session 2**: none dedicated — a security smell gets named in passing if one shows up in the demo's diff
- **Session 3**: sandboxing, permission models, why tools have allowlists/denylists
- **Session 4**: none dedicated — trust boundaries, prompt injection and supply chain moved out of this session and **landed in Session 5**, which now closes the thread with a block of its own
- **Session 5**: the block that closes the thread. Threat models (prompt injection from repo content, malicious extensions/skills/MCP servers, the agent's own destructive mistakes, credential exfiltration), permission models as a design space, and the sandbox ladder. Placed after the hands-on so it lands on an extension they just wrote and installed themselves.
- **Session 6**: self-hosting makes *you* the operator — runtime, patching, machine, quality — and "local" does not automatically mean private, since the agent still calls out. **Narrowed deliberately**: the open-weight block now follows Copes's arc, which covers those two and not the model supply chain or injection, so the session no longer promises them.

## Proposed Sessions

> ### Base course — sessions 1-4
>
> The fundamentals arc: *how do I work well with this thing?* Each session adds a layer of structure, and Session 4 closes the arc.

### Session 1: The Vibe Coding Experience

# Sesión 4 — Context Engineering (Notas para el instructor)

> A cargo: Agus. Estado: borrador. Todo el material de la sesión está en español.

## Objetivo de la sesión (en una frase)

Que salgan sabiendo **mantener documentos vivos del proyecto**, que separan el problema de la solución y registran las decisiones, y usarlos como contexto para planificar y construir.

## Audiencia y supuestos

- **Dura 2 horas y no se instala nada.**
- **Con qué llegan**: su proyecto, un `AGENTS.md`, al menos un skill, y la feature de la tarea de la Sesión 3: una que no pueden describir en una frase. Si alguien no la trajo, que la elija durante el recap.
- Grupo heterogéneo, de primer año a graduados.
- El riesgo de la clase no es técnico: es que documentar se sienta como tarea escolar. Los dos bloques prácticos terminan con el agente usando los docs; ese contraste es lo que lo evita.

## Plan tema por tema

### Recap (~10 min)

Discusión, no slides. Dos disparadores:

**1. Show-and-tell de skills.** ¿Alguien creó un skill nuevo durante la semana? ¿Encontró alguno hecho que le sirvió? Dos o tres casos alcanzan. Preguntar por el criterio: qué convirtieron en skill y qué dejaron en el `AGENTS.md`.

**2. ¿Qué dudas quedaron de la Sesión 3?** Pregunta abierta. MCP y subagentes suelen dejar preguntas sueltas.

### Qué vamos a ver hoy (~5 min)

El encuadre: en la Sesión 2 escribieron un plan por tarea, en la Sesión 3 la configuración que no cambia. Hoy escriben documentos del proyecto que alimentan los planes y registran las decisiones.

Los dos conceptos que enmarcan la sesión, presentados acá y retomados en el cierre:

- **Deuda cognitiva**: el costo mental de delegar de forma repetida el razonamiento, la memoria y la resolución de problemas en la IA. Cada decisión que no tomaste vos es una decisión que no entendés.
- **Rendición cognitiva**: el paso siguiente: aceptar lo que el agente produce sin leerlo de verdad, y adoptar sus decisiones como propias. Cuando no entendés el problema en profundidad, las respuestas del agente se convierten en tu opinión, porque no tenés con qué contrastarlas.

La frase de la sesión:

> *"Documentar es pensar antes de construir."*

### Dos dominios (~15 min)

Ejemplo primero, concepto después. El ejemplo es **una sola feature**: agregar soporte multi-usuario a la lista de tareas (el proyecto A de la Sesión 1, el mismo del ejercicio de la Sesión 3). La misma feature descrita dos veces:

- **Dominio del problema**: la necesidad. Varias personas quieren usar la lista y cada una quiere ver solo lo suyo. Se detalla con herramientas del lado del problema:
  - **Actores**: quién usa el sistema (usuario registrado, visitante).
  - **Datos y relaciones**: qué cosas existen y cómo se conectan (usuario, tarea, cada tarea pertenece a un usuario).
  - **Procesos**: qué hace cada actor (registrarse, entrar, trabajar sobre sus tareas).

  Todo en términos del problema, sin hablar del sistema. La charla que originó el framework hablaba de procesos del día a día porque la audiencia no era técnica; acá la audiencia es técnica y los problemas son problemas en general, no solo procesos.

- **Dominio de la solución**: el sistema que resuelve esa necesidad. Se detalla con herramientas del lado de la solución:
  - **Diagramas de datos**: la tabla `users`, el `user_id` en `tasks`.
  - **Breadboards o bocetos de pantallas**: registro, login, el header con la sesión.
  - **Flujos**: el usuario entra, la sesión se valida, la lista se filtra.

  Es **una** de las muchas formas posibles de resolver esa necesidad.

Las dos ideas que tienen que quedar:

1. **El mismo problema admite muchas soluciones.** Si arrancás por la solución, el riesgo es doble: tomás decisiones sin haber considerado el problema en profundidad, y muchas de esas decisiones las termina derivando el agente, que por defecto devuelve la respuesta promedio de todo el conocimiento que ya tiene.
2. **La distinción importa con o sin IA.** Es la separación de siempre entre requerimientos y diseño.

Cierre del bloque, pregunta a la sala: ¿dónde vive esta distinción en el proyecto de ustedes hoy? En ningún lado: el código es todo dominio de la solución, y el problema quedó en el historial de chats. Eso abre el bloque siguiente.

### Documentar lo que ya construiste (~30 min)

~5 de plantillas, ~25 de práctica.

**Las plantillas (~5 min).** Dos tipos de documento, commiteados en el repo:

`docs/PROJECT.md`, uno solo. La descripción general del proyecto:

```markdown
# <Proyecto>

Qué es el proyecto y para quién.

## Objetivo
El objetivo principal: qué tiene que lograr para valer la pena.

## Restricciones
Lo que ya está decidido y no se rediscute por feature:
stack, límites, supuestos.
```

`docs/features/<nombre>.md`, uno por feature:

```markdown
# <Feature>

El problema que resuelve: qué necesidad cubre y qué tiene que
poder hacer quien la usa.

## Diseño

### Modelo
Los datos en juego: entidades, campos, relaciones.

### Flujo: <nombre>
Uno por interacción: las pantallas que recorre y qué se puede
hacer en cada una, los pasos, las reglas que se validan, y las
decisiones que se tomaron en el camino, cada una con su motivo.
```

Dos cosas para decir sobre las plantillas:

- **Son plantillas, no formularios.** Cada proyecto las adapta: se borran secciones que sobran, se agregan las que faltan. El error es dejarlas como vinieron.
- **Relación con el `AGENTS.md`.** Algo de superposición puede haber, pero idealmente el `AGENTS.md` apunta a estos documentos: él lleva lo operativo de cada turno (comandos, convenciones) y referencia los docs para el entendimiento del proyecto.

**El trabajo (~25 min).** Documentar el proyecto que ya tienen, de forma interactiva: el agente explora el código, el historial de commits y los planes de las sesiones anteriores, muestra un borrador del `PROJECT.md` y de un `<feature>.md` por cada feature existente, y pregunta lo que no puede saber: el problema que se quiso resolver y el porqué de cada decisión. El estudiante responde y el doc final sale de esa conversación.

Qué vigilar caminando la sala:

- **El problema, primero.** Tiene que describir qué se quiere resolver con la feature, no cómo está construida. Si arranca con tablas o componentes, quedó en el dominio equivocado.
- **Las decisiones, dentro de cada flujo.** Si no hay ninguna o dicen generalidades ("elegimos React por su popularidad"), el ejercicio no se hizo. Las decisiones reales tienen la forma "el estado vive en el server y no en el cliente porque X". Varias ni las tomaron ellos: las tomó el agente en la Sesión 1. Eso se decide ahora, en retrospectiva.

### Pausa (~5 min)

Dejar proyectadas las plantillas.

### Documentar la próxima feature e implementarla (~40 min)

Explicación corta (~5) y el resto trabajo continuo: doc → plan → implementación.

**La explicación (~5 min).** Toman la feature que trajeron. Puede ser nueva o una modificación de una existente; en el segundo caso extienden el doc que esa feature ya tiene. Escriben o actualizan su `docs/features/<nombre>.md` antes de tocar código. Tres instrucciones:

1. **No le pidas el documento: pedile que te haga preguntas.** Contale el problema con tus palabras y que te interrogue. Las preguntas exponen lo que dabas por sentado y no estaba escrito. El borrador se escribe después, cuando las decisiones están tomadas. Hay un skill hecho para esto: [grill-me](https://github.com/mattpocock/skills/blob/main/skills/productivity/grill-me/SKILL.md) de Matt Pocock, que entrevista hasta resolver el árbol de decisiones. Es un `SKILL.md` como los de la Sesión 3.
2. **El documento es de alto nivel.** Si la feature toca una librería o una API, context7 (Sesión 3) sirve para entenderla, pero los detalles de implementación no van al doc: van al plan que sale después.
3. **El doc alimenta el plan.** La cadena completa: doc → plan → implementación → review. El plan sale con las decisiones ya tomadas, y el review compara contra dos cosas: el plan (¿hizo lo que acordamos?) y el doc (¿respeta las decisiones del proyecto?).

**El trabajo (~35 min).** Escribir el doc de la feature vía interrogación, generar el plan con Plannotator partiendo del doc, ejecutar. No hace falta terminar la implementación; alcanza con generar el plan desde el doc.

Qué vigilar caminando la sala:

- Que la interrogación sea real. Preguntarle al estudiante: ¿qué pregunta te hizo el agente que no tenías respondida? Si no hay ninguna, le pidió el documento directo y no hay ninguna decisión propia adentro.
- Que el plan cite el doc. Si el plan contradice una decisión escrita, mostrarlo: es el doc funcionando como criterio de review.

**Extra: orquestación (~5 min, opcional, mientras trabajan).** Una vuelta por la sala o una slide fija para los que van rápido. Con los docs en el repo hay una fuente de verdad compartida, y eso habilita varios agentes a la vez: un subagente implementa mientras otro revisa contra el doc, o dos features en paralelo con worktrees.

### Cierre (~15 min)

- **¿Qué cambió cuando el agente tuvo el doc?** Casos concretos: qué preguntó el agente en la interrogación, qué hizo el plan distinto.
- **Deuda y rendición cognitiva, de vuelta.** La diferencia entre delegar la escritura y delegar el pensamiento. Si el doc lo escribió el agente sin preguntarte nada, delegaste las dos cosas.
- **Cuándo no usar IA.** La IA amplifica lo que ya sabés; sin los fundamentos, amplifica la confusión. "Don't use AI as a crutch" (MIT Missing Semester).
- **Ser dueño.** Entender, decidir, discutir, mantener. Si no podés explicar tu sistema sin abrir el código, no sos dueño del sistema.
- **Nombrar la transición**: con esta sesión termina el tramo de "cómo trabajo bien con esta herramienta". Las próximas dos desarman la máquina: la Sesión 5 abre el harness por adentro y la Sesión 6 cambia el modelo que tiene abajo.
- **Recordar la demo**: la Sesión 5 abre con **una hora de demos del proyecto**. Se anunció en la Sesión 1 y ésta es la última clase antes. El que quiera mostrar, que venga con el repo listo y sepa qué quiere contar en 5 a 7 minutos. No es una entrega, es voluntario y no se corrige.
- **Tarea**: mantener los docs vivos durante la semana. Cada decisión nueva va al doc de su feature; anotar cuándo los docs sirvieron y cuándo quedaron desactualizados respecto del código.

## Timing de la sesión (~2 h)

| Bloque | Tiempo |
|---|---|
| Recap | 10 min |
| Qué vamos a ver hoy | 5 min |
| Dos dominios | 15 min |
| Documentar lo que ya construiste (plantillas + trabajo) | 30 min |
| Pausa | 5 min |
| Documentar la próxima feature e implementarla | 40 min |
| Cierre | 15 min |

## Herramientas y recursos referenciados

- Nada nuevo que instalar. Se usan [Plannotator](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@plannotator/pi-extension) (Sesión 2), [`pi-subagents`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/pi-subagents) (Sesión 2) y [context7](https://context7.com/) vía `pi-mcp-adapter` (Sesión 3).
- [grill-me](https://github.com/mattpocock/skills/blob/main/skills/productivity/grill-me/SKILL.md), el skill de Matt Pocock que entrevista sobre una idea hasta resolver el árbol de decisiones. Opcional para el bloque de 40.
- "Your Brain on ChatGPT: Accumulation of Cognitive Debt when Using an AI Assistant for Essay Writing Task" (MIT Media Lab, 2025), la fuente del término deuda cognitiva. Es un estudio chico y sobre ensayos, no sobre código: usar el término, no sobrevender el paper.
- MIT Missing Semester 2026, clase de agentic coding: "don't use AI as a crutch", ya citado en la Sesión 1.
- La charla interna de Filadd "Documentando para entender" (2026-08-14), la fuente del framework de dos dominios. No es material público.

## Pendientes (para próximas iteraciones)

- **Preparar el ejemplo de dos dominios** (multi-usuario en la lista de tareas) sobre el proyecto demo, con los diagramas y breadboards de los dos lados listos para mostrar.
- **Probar grill-me en Pi** con el proyecto demo: confirmar que el skill carga y que la interrogación funciona como en Claude Code.
- **Escribir los dos prompts/skills de la sesión** (los TODO del ejercicio): el de exploración interactiva de la Parte 1 (el agente explora, muestra un borrador y pregunta lo que no puede saber) y el de interrogación de la Parte 2, basado en grill-me.

# From Vibe Coding to Agentic Engineering

6-week course for university CS students on the full spectrum of AI-assisted development — from pure vibe coding to structured agentic engineering. FaMAF extension course.

> **Source of truth**: the repo `filadd/agentic-engineering-famaf-extension-course`. Session artifacts here (`INSTRUCTOR.md`, `slides.md`, `exercise/README.md`) are mirrors — edit them in the repo, not here. The `session-N.md` notes are vault-native.
>
> **Mirror state, 2026-10-25.** Session artifacts mirror `main` at `d76389f` (PRs #14 and #15 merged), except Session 3's files and Session 5's `INSTRUCTOR.md`, which mirror the open PR #16 (`feature/session-3-deck`, worktree `~/workspace/filadd/.worktrees/agentic-course-session-3`). Session 2 also carries `prompts.md`, added on `main` after the merge. [[topic-inventory]] still matches `main`'s `COURSE_PROGRAM.md` tiers. The Session 1 PDF export, the HTML decks (`sessions/session-{1,2,3}/deck/index.html`), Session 5's `propuesta-mcp/` deck, Session 2's vibe-coded demo app and its replay (`sessions/session-2/{app,replay}/`) and the `session-replay` skill (`.claude/skills/`) stay in the repo only.
>
> The repo folded the standalone tier notes into `COURSE_PROGRAM.md` and dropped `resources/`, so [[topic-inventory]] now mirrors that file directly.
>
> **Session materials are in Spanish, instructor notes included**, for every session except Session 5's `INSTRUCTOR.md`. Session 1 switched to Spanish in PR #10. These vault `session-N.md` notes stay in English.

## Format

- 6 sessions, 1 per week, in two arcs — **base (1-4)**: *how do I work well with this thing?*, closed by Session 4; **advanced (5-6)**: *what is this made of, and what if I swap its parts?*, closed by Session 6. Same cohort throughout; the split is announced to students in Session 1
- **Session 1 is 3 hours; the rest are 2** — the extra hour buys introductions, the fundamentals block, and the Pi install
- Theory → hands-on → show-and-tell discussion
- Same project across all sessions; must run in the browser. Students bring their own idea — Session 1 now ships `proyecto-de-respaldo` for those who don't
- Tool: **Pi** (`pi.dev`) — decided. Students install it in Session 1
- Class size: ~30 students, quota of 35. Audience widened in PR #10 to advanced CS students *and* junior programmers

## People

## Key Thesis

Vibe coding is a great on-ramp, but professional software development demands accountability. The course shows *why* each level of structure matters by letting students experience the failures firsthand before introducing the solutions.

**Core mental model: "Managing a smart intern."**

**Companion idea: responsibility stays with the person.** If it breaks, if a key leaks, if the code is unmaintainable — you are accountable, not the AI. "The agent wrote it" is not an excuse that exists.

## The Spectrum

1. Vibe Coding — prompt-and-accept, no code review
2. AI-Assisted Coding — copilot completions, developer maintains control
3. Directed AI Assistance — experienced use with constraints, specs, review
4. Agentic Coding — orchestrating AI agents on tasks with oversight
5. Agentic Engineering — full discipline: specs, quality gates, multi-agent coordination

# Kurasu (クラス) — virtual class platform

New project built in the context of [[vibe-coding-to-agentic-engineering|the agentic engineering course]]. A virtual class tool that serves two roles: the running example for the course, and the actual tool the course itself runs on.

**Status:** live in production at https://kurasu.asermax.com, with classes 1 and 2 loaded and the professors registered. Built on 2026-10-18/19 with the mahou workflow (explore → shape → design → program design → test design → implement), and recorded as the agentic demo for session 2. Last deploy: 2026-10-19 from `7772c32` (visual adjustments round).

## Where it lives

- Code: `app/` inside `~/workspace/filadd/agentic-engineering-famaf-extension-course` (pnpm + turbo monorepo, package name `kurasu`)
- Branch: `main` (first build and visual adjustments merged through PR #14 on 2026-10-20)
- Docs: `app/docs/architecture/` (in Spanish: data model, data access, components, login and access, real-time classroom, slides API, poll/session states, web loading and actions, session news by mail, invariants) and HTML prototypes in `app/docs/prototipos/`
- Agent wiki: `.mahou/wiki/` (backend architecture rules, API shape, web patterns, lint/test fence)
- Work logs: `.scratch/aula-virtual/` (first build), `.scratch/ajustes-visuales/` (loading states and action feedback) and `.scratch/backlog-kurasu/` (session news by mail), each with `status.md` and `tasks.md`

## What it does

- **Students**: register via QR code → email → magic link, pick an animal avatar; home lists the featured session and earlier ones with their material, polls and questions; the classroom shows the professor's slides in sync, with polls, questions, raised hands and material in a side panel; responsive for phone and desktop; dark mode
- **Professors**: desktop admin to create and reorder sessions, upload material (an HTML file can be marked as slides and is checked against the slides API), run polls (multiple choice, word cloud, scale), manage users and the registration code
- **Session news by mail**: enabling a session, uploading material and opening a poll record a pending news entry for the session; the professor sees them in the session's Contenido tab, discards them or picks some and writes an announcement, which the API mails to everyone with access (professor in To, students in Bcc batches of 49), linking to the session on the student home
- **Real time**: one Durable Object per session pushes changes over WebSocket and tracks who is present
- **Slides API**: the web tells the slides HTML which slide and step to show, and relays the professor's position to the students; session 2's deck already runs on it

## Stack

All on Cloudflare, deployed with Alchemy 2 (`pnpm deploy`, stage `prod`):

- Web: TanStack Start (SPA) + Router + React Query, React 19, Tailwind 4
- Storage: D1 for data, R2 for material files; secrets through varlock
- Tooling: TypeScript 7 (tsgo), oxlint + oxfmt, vitest, lefthook; API tests run against a local Alchemy stack

I've pulled both repos (the course repo was already up to date). Session 4 has the least material of any session so far, and the vault mirror is behind the repo in a few places.

## Session 4 in the repo

- **What exists:** `INSTRUCTOR.md`, `slides.md` and `exercise/README.md`, all from PR #8 in August and marked as a draft. Sessions 1–3 each have an animated HTML deck that runs on kurasu's slides API; Session 4 has none, and no example project is prepared.
- **Plan in the notes:** two hands-on blocks that make up 70 of the 120 minutes. In the first, students document their existing project (`docs/PROJECT.md` plus one `docs/features/<name>.md` per feature). In the second, they document the next feature by having the agent interrogate them (grill-me), then go doc → plan → implementation.
- **Open items in `INSTRUCTOR.md`:**
  - The two-domains example (multi-user to-do list) isn't built.
  - grill-me hasn't been tested in Pi.
  - The two exercise prompts/skills are still TODOs.
- **Subagents question is still open.** Session 3 now teaches subagents (PR #16, merged). `COURSE_PROGRAM.md` and Session 4's files still say Session 4 introduces them. Session 4's exercise doesn't mention them, and its orchestration aside names worktrees, which Session 3 declared out of the course.
- **Cost/tokens may not be covered anywhere now.** The vault says Session 4 closes the base arc with cost, limits, career and atrophy. But `session-4.md` lists cost/tokens as dropped from the closing. Session 3 removed its "Nada de esto es gratis" slide on Oct 26, and that slide was where the cost of context lived.

## Vault drift (`01_Projects/vibe-coding-to-agentic-engineering`)

- **Session 3 `INSTRUCTOR.md` and `slides.md`** are behind the repo by the Oct 25–26 commits: the "Nada de esto es gratis" slide was removed, plus the AGENTS.md-as-index slide, Notion MCP instead of Linear, and the example skill/agent repo slides. Every other mirrored file is identical.
- **`README.md`** still says PR #16 is open, `origin/main` is at `d76389f`, and "the course has not run yet". PRs #16–#19 are all merged now, and kurasu already carries classes 1 and 2.
- **The kurasu note** (`01_Projects/kurasu/index.md`) was last updated Oct 20. It doesn't record email validation (#17), the session feedback poll (#18, which was in its own idea backlog) or questions on the featured card (#19, merged today). It also doesn't know about the new `.scratch/` logs (`email-valido`, `feedback-de-sesion`, `preguntas-en-la-card`).
- **Possible Session 4 reading** added since Oct 25: the Phoenix Architecture notes, and the archived articles "When does a specification become a program", "Context inertia when agents won't let go" and "Chasing the Karpathy peak".

## Show-and-tell: your process covers the session plan

Your mahou runs on kurasu already cover almost every point of the planned session, with real artifacts. `preguntas-en-la-card` is the best example: it went from explore to merge in one run and every stage left files in `.scratch/preguntas-en-la-card/`.

| Session 4 point | What you'd show |
|---|---|
| Problem vs. solution domain | `shape.md` (behavior and decisions) next to `design.md` (data model, flows, rules) |
| Interrogate before writing the doc | The design-tree rounds. `decisions.md` holds 39 decisions from the exploration, including the ones replaced along the way |
| Living project docs, `AGENTS.md` points to them | `app/AGENTS.md` → `app/docs/architecture/`, and the PR #19 commit that reconciled the docs with what was built |
| doc → plan → implement → review | Program design and test design → `implement/` → agentic review rounds → `implementation-status.md` |
| Subagents / orchestration (the open question) | One subagent per repo, scouts, facet reviewers. This would close the subagents question with a concrete use, without teaching the primitive a second time |
| Cognitive debt / surrender | You settled every leaf yourself. The first kurasu build had 124 product decisions |

A possible 2 h outline:
1. Recap (10 min).
2. Two domains (15 min), with kurasu as the example instead of the to-do list that was never built.
3. Walk through `preguntas-en-la-card` stage by stage (~50 min).
4. A short live piece (~25 min): run a shape or design round on a small backlog item in front of the room, so they see the questions happen. "Professor-only messages" from the kurasu backlog is a candidate.
5. Closing block as planned (15 min).

This turns the two hands-on blocks into demonstration. If you still want students to leave with their own `docs/`, the first exercise could become homework.

The `preguntas-en-la-card` status says PR #19 still needs a manual `pnpm deploy`. That matters if you want to use the featured card's questions during the class.

38	Vibe coding is a great on-ramp, but professional software development demands accountability. The course shows *why* each level of structure matters by letting students experience the failures firsthand before introducing the solutions.

41	
42	**Companion idea: responsibility stays with the person.** If it breaks, if a key leaks, if the code is unmaintainable — you are accountable, not the AI. "The agent wrote it" is not an excuse that exists.

28

Turn what you keep re-explaining to the agent into configuration it reads on its own. The line the session runs on: *"lo que le explicaste dos veces, escribilo una."*

Underneath it, a second idea: **everything you add to the agent is paid for in context.** The opening slide makes it a budget — a 200k context bar where `AGENTS.md` (~2k global + repo), 20 skill descriptions, Playwright MCP (~13.7k) and Context7 (~2k) add up to ~11% of the window.

Four artifacts, one move — **what isn't needed every turn leaves the window until it's needed**: `AGENTS.md` (always loaded), skills (on demand), MCP tools (`exposure` decides), subagents (a whole job in another context). The closing table lands it and stays projected while the práctica starts.

The three formats of the day — `AGENTS.md`, Agent Skills, MCP — are **open standards in the same home**: the AAIF (Linux Foundation). OpenAI donated `AGENTS.md` and Anthropic MCP when the foundation formed (Dec 2025); Agent Skills followed in Oct 2026. The point for the room: nothing you write today is tied to Pi, and competing companies donated all three.

**Pi 1.0 ships MCP built in.** No adapter, no tool-proxy story: servers are declared in `.pi/mcp.json` (or `~/.pi/agent/mcp.json`), and what reaches the model is decided by `exposure` — `codemode` (default: tools called from a script, only the result comes back), `deferred` (`tool_search`), `direct` (all definitions — Playwright's 13.7k), `hidden`. i was thinking:
- write a short set of slides with some main concepts: diseño del problem, diseño de la solución, documentación, subagentes, maybe something else?
- jump in between those and working on a new feature using my mahou skills (e.g. a chat on the classroom of kurasu)

what do you think, does it fit?

Yes, it fits, and I think it works better than walking through a finished run. Session 4 is about thinking about the problem before the solution and keeping the decisions written down. A live run lets students watch you make those decisions as they come up. With a finished run, they only see the results.

## What I'd adjust

**Size the goal to two hours.** The kurasu runs took a day or more each, so a chat won't get from explore to merged in one class. A realistic target is explore → shape → design, with the docs written. If time allows, add a program design or implement one thin slice with subagents. The session's material is in the first half of the workflow anyway, and implement is mostly waiting.

**Let the room answer the design-tree questions.** When shape asks something like "can students edit or delete their messages?" or "does the professor moderate?", put it to the class, or open a poll in kurasu itself. That turns "interrogate before you write" into something they do, and they leave having made decisions themselves. That matters for the cognitive surrender point.

**Do a dry run beforehand.** Run it once on your own to time each stage and find where it gets stuck. Keep that run's artifacts on a branch. If the live run stalls (network, a slow model, a long tangent), you can continue from what the dry run produced.

**Give the hands-on a replacement.** The current goal is for students to leave with their own `docs/`. Without a practice block, that has to become homework: document the project with the two templates and interrogate one feature. That also feeds the Session 5 demos.

## Concepts for the slides

On top of the four you listed:

- **`AGENTS.md` as an index.** Session 3's deck promises you'll cover this ("Agus lo cuenta en la próxima clase"), so it has to be there. `app/AGENTS.md` → `app/docs/` is the example.
- **Deuda y rendición cognitiva.** This is the session's frame, and it's what you show by having the room decide.
- **The closing judgment material:** cost, when not to use AI, atrophy, ownership. Session 4 closes the base arc, so this can't move to session 6. You can cover cost live by showing how much context and money the run used by the end.

Each concept can come back at the stage where it shows up:

| Concept | When it comes up live |
|---|---|
| Diseño del problema | explore / shape on the canvas |
| Diseño de la solución | design: data model, flows, a prototype of the chat panel |
| Subagentes | the scouts during explore, then implement / reviewers if you get there |
| Documentación | write-documentation, and how the notes in `app/docs/` change |
| Review / verification (callback to Session 2) | test design: the doc becomes the review criterion |

## A possible timing

| Block | Time |
|---|---|
| Recap + why we do this live | 10 |
| Problema vs. solución, deuda cognitiva (slides) | 10 |
| Live: explore + shape, room answers | 30 |
| Pausa | 5 |
| Slides: diseño de la solución + documentación + `AGENTS.md` as index | 10 |
| Live: design + docs | 25 |
| Subagentes (slide + whatever implement/review shows) | 10 |
| Closing: cost of the run, when not to use AI, ownership, homework, demo reminder | 15 |

Questions get answered as they come up, mostly while the agent is working.

## Picking the chat feature

A chat in the classroom is a good choice. It builds on the real-time Durable Object that's already there, and it has real decisions to make: who can write, moderation, whether messages persist after the session, how a message differs from the existing questions. The backlog idea of professor-only messages overlaps with it, and that overlap is itself a good question for the room.

The one thing that only you can settle is the scope. A full chat could take the whole class in shape. If you want to reach design, frame it as "chat for the featured session" from the start.

If this matches what you had in mind, I can rewrite Session 4's `INSTRUCTOR.md` and `slides.md` around this format next.

# kurasu: docs

## What each folder holds

| Folder | Holds | Index |
|---|---|---|
| architecture/ | the shape of the system and how each part works | [Architecture](architecture/README.md) |
| prototipos/ | no notes, only the HTML prototypes of the screens that the notes link to | [Prototipos](prototipos/README.md) |

There is a single note folder, so every note goes in `architecture/`, whatever part of the system it explains.

`_templates/` holds no notes. The underscore is a sorting convention and nothing more: it floats the folder to the top of the file explorer.

`prototipos/` holds no notes either: it holds the HTML prototypes of the screens, and each one is linked from the note that describes its screen.

## Naming

A note is named after the aspect it explains, in kebab-case. Not after its folder, not numbered, not dated: a date is a frontmatter field, so an index can sort on it without every filename carrying one.

File names are unique across the whole docs folder, so a link never has to be disambiguated. Before adding a note, check the name is not taken.

Every folder's index is called `README.md`, so that name is the one deliberate collision here: the payoff is that each index renders as a folder front page when the repository is browsed on the web. A link to a folder's index names the folder: `[the technical design](technical-design/README.md)`.

## Frontmatter

Every note carries `title` and `summary`, plus `created`. The summary is what shows up in search, in hover previews and in the indexes, so write it as a sentence about the subject rather than about the note.

## Invariants

[`architecture/invariantes.md`](architecture/invariantes.md) lists the rules every change respects. The mahou skills read it before settling or proposing anything and check each decision against it. Add a rule when it holds beyond the change that surfaced it, and link the note that explains it when the reason needs more than a sentence.

## How to write a note

**A note explains how one part works.** It opens with an overview a reader can stop after, then the mechanism: the shape of the data, what calls what, in what order, with a diagram when the subject is a flow, a tree or a sequence. A reader should be able to hold that part of the system in their head without opening `src/` first.

`_templates/note.md` offers the sections a note can use. They are a menu, not a required shape and not a closed list: keep the ones the subject needs, add one the menu lacks when the subject asks for it, and order them so the note is easiest to follow rather than in the order the template lists them. Edge cases and failure modes go in the prose or in a callout, never in a section of their own.

**Reasoning goes in a callout, beside the thing it justifies**, not as the spine of the note:

```markdown
> [!NOTE] Why it is this way and not the obvious alternative
> The reasoning, next to the mechanism it justifies.
```

A note that opens with the argument for a design makes the reader meet the case for the architecture before the architecture itself, and the argument is not what they came for. It is still worth keeping (it is what lets a decision be revisited rather than re-argued); it just is not the spine. Per-decision *why* is also the one thing the code already has, densely, at the point of each decision; what code cannot give anyone is the shape of the whole.

# Architecture

This folder holds the shape of the system and how each part works. Each note explains one part of it; the reasoning behind a choice sits in a callout next to the mechanism it justifies. See [the docs charter](../README.md) for how a note is written.

## What notes exist

One row per note, kept by hand: adding a note here is part of writing it.

| Note | Explains |
|---|---|
| [Modelo de datos](modelo-de-datos.md) | Las entidades que kurasu guarda en D1: usuarios, sesiones con su material, encuestas, preguntas, manos levantadas y novedades pendientes, y los códigos de registro y de los links del mail. |
| [Acceso a datos](acceso-a-datos.md) | Cómo la API lee y escribe en D1: el repositorio común sobre cada tabla, los puertos que el core declara con sus operaciones, las queries propias de cada store, y los límites de filas y de parámetros. |
| [Componentes](componentes.md) | Las piezas de kurasu y cómo se hablan: la web en el navegador, la API y el aula en Cloudflare, D1, R2, Email Sending y el estado que guarda el navegador. |
| [Login y acceso](login-y-acceso.md) | Cómo un usuario se registra y entra con un magic link, cómo la API revisa el acceso en cada pedido y cómo el profe administra los usuarios y el código de registro. |
| [Tiempo real del aula](tiempo-real-del-aula.md) | Cómo el aula de cada sesión avisa al instante sus cambios, quién cuenta como presente, qué pasa cuando se corta la conexión y cómo se comporta la pantalla del aula. |
| [API de las slides](api-de-las-slides.md) | Cómo la web le dice al HTML de las slides a qué slide y paso ir, cómo viaja la posición del profe hasta los estudiantes y cómo se revisa que un HTML respete la API al marcarlo como slides, desde el modal de subida o desde la lista del material. |
| [Estados de encuestas y sesiones, y sus pantallas](estados-de-encuestas-y-sesiones.md) | Los ciclos de vida de las encuestas, las sesiones, la sesión destacada, las preguntas destacadas y las preguntas, qué ve el estudiante en su inicio, cómo maneja el profe las sesiones desde el admin. |
| [Carga y acciones de la web](carga-y-acciones-de-la-web.md) | Cómo la web dibuja una pantalla mientras cargan sus datos, qué muestra cuando la carga falla y cómo responde a cada acción del usuario, al instante o en espera. |
| [Novedades por mail](novedades-por-mail.md) | Cómo kurasu registra lo nuevo de cada sesión como novedades pendientes, cómo el profe elige cuáles anunciar desde el admin de la sesión y cómo la API manda el anuncio por mail a los usuarios con acceso. |
| [Feedback de una sesión](feedback-de-sesion.md) | Cómo un alumno deja un puntaje de emojis y un comentario libre sobre una sesión, qué guarda esa respuesta y cómo el profe lee todas las respuestas con el nombre de cada alumno. |
| [Invariantes](invariantes.md) | Las reglas que respeta todo cambio en kurasu, sobre cómo se comporta el producto y cómo está armado el sistema. |

Honest gaps, so nobody assumes coverage that is not there. Name the part, and say where its behaviour is currently documented instead: in code comments, in a commit message, or nowhere.

It imports no adapter and nothing from Cloudflare, Alchemy, Drizzle or jose. - Adapters live outside core: the D1 adapters in `packages/database`, the R2, Email Sending, JWT and Durable Object adapters in `apps/api`. The apps wire the core services to their adapters; packages never import apps. - Expected failures are typed errors declared with Schema; the code does not catch defects as if they were expected. - Decode everything that enters at a boundary (a request body, a stored row, a message) with its schema before using it. - The Worker reads configuration with Effect `Config` where it is built and passes it to the layers as plain values (`Access.layer(webOrigin)`, `JoseSessionTokens(jwtSecret)`). Secrets come from varlock: `.env.schema` declares them and `.env.local`, out of git, holds them. The API Worker builds its HTTP app, with every layer that reads D1, inside `fetch`, because the bindings exist only when the isolate starts (see `alchemy/local-dev`). - Reads are bounded (a list has a maximum) and paginate by key, not by offset. - D1 has no transactions: writes that must land together go in one batch. ## Sources - `.scratch/aula-virtual/program-design/kurasu.md`, branches 1 to 4 and Standards. ----- # Implement in kurasu - **Tracker**: an Entire trail per change, created with `entire trail create --no-branch --type feature`. The trail's description holds the change's tasks as a markdown checklist, one `- [ ]` line per task with what it requires. There is no local task list. - **Reaching it**: `entire trail show

--json` reads the description; `entire trail update

--body "…"` writes it, and replaces the whole description, so read it first and write it back whole. - **States**: a task is pending as `- [ ]` and done as `- [x]`. It is marked done when its change is implemented, tested and committed. There is no in-progress state. The trail goes to `--status closed` when its branch is merged. - **Description format**: Entire stores the description as plain text: it drops list dashes, bold, backticks, headings and blank lines, and keeps the `[ ]`/`[x]` marks. It keeps line breaks only when the body is written as a markdown list: write each task as `- [ ] `, with a blank line around the `Tareas` heading line. A body of bare `[ ]` lines comes back as one paragraph. - **Branch**: the trail is created without a branch. Once the change's branch is pushed, and before its pull request is opened, link it with `entire trail link

--branch `. A pull request whose branch belongs to no trail makes Entire create a new trail for it. - **Sessions on the trail**: a trail shows the checkpoints of its branch, and a checkpoint is a session attached to a commit through an `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer. Entire records no session on its own during an implement run. Every subagent inherits `ENTIRE_PI_NESTED=1` from the supervisor, and the project's Entire extension for pi then forwards nothing, so the subagents' commits carry no trailer. The supervisor runs on `main` and commits nothing on the branch. When the run ends, before the branch is pushed, attach every session from a checkout on the branch: - Each subagent's transcript stays in `~/.pi/agent/sessions/----/` after its worktree is removed; the first user message of each names its job. - Attach each subagent to the last commit it made: `entire session attach --agent pi --commit --force`. Attach the reviewers a review dispatched, and the review session itself, to the review's last commit with `--review`. A session that made no commit goes on the commit of the stage it served. - Attach the supervisor last, to the branch's last commit: `entire session attach $PI_SESSION_ID --agent pi --commit --force`. - Each attach to a commit without a checkpoint rewrites that commit and every later one; the content stays. Look up each commit by its subject, not by an earlier hash. A second session on the same commit joins its checkpoint without a rewrite. - Without a terminal, `attach` only prints what it would do; `--force` applies it. This rule is the user's go-ahead for unpushed commits on the change's branch. - The sessions show on the trail once the branch is linked. - **Closing**: close the trail with `entire trail update

# Sesión 4 — Context Engineering (Notas para el instructor)

> A cargo: Agus. Estado: borrador. Todo el material de la sesión está en español.

## Objetivo de la sesión (en una frase)

Que vean, sobre un proyecto real y en vivo, cómo se separa el problema de la solución, cómo se mantienen documentos vivos que registran las decisiones y cómo esos documentos y los subagentes sostienen el contexto del agente, para que lo repliquen en su proyecto durante la semana.

## Formato

La sesión es una **demostración en vivo con slides de conceptos**. No hay práctica en clase: la práctica es la tarea.

- **El deck** (`deck/index.html`) lleva solo conceptos. No menciona las partes en vivo y se puede mirar después como resumen.
- **La parte en vivo** es una feature nueva de kurasu, el aula virtual del curso: **un chat en el aula de la sesión destacada**. Se trabaja con los skills de mahou (explore, shape, design, write-documentation y, si da el tiempo, program design o implement), proyectando la terminal y el canvas.
- **Se alterna**: un bloque de slides presenta un concepto y enseguida se lo ve aplicado en el trabajo en vivo.
- **Las preguntas se contestan cuando salen.** Los ratos en que el agente está trabajando son el momento natural para hacerlo.

## Audiencia y supuestos

- **Dura 2 horas y no se instala nada.**
- **Con qué llegan**: su proyecto, un `AGENTS.md`, al menos un skill, las notas de la tarea de la Sesión 3 (qué le tuvieron que explicar igual al agente) y una feature que no pueden describir en una frase. Las dos últimas alimentan la tarea de esta semana.
- Grupo heterogéneo, de primer año a graduados.
- **Ya vieron kurasu**: es el aula donde siguen las slides, y la Sesión 2 mostró la grabación de cómo se construyó. Hoy ven el proceso en vivo, con las decisiones tomándose en el momento.

## Plan tema por tema

### Recap

Slides 1 a 3. Discusión, no slides. Tres disparadores:

1. **¿Creaste o encontraste un skill nuevo?** Dos o tres casos. Preguntar por el criterio: qué convirtieron en skill y qué dejaron en el `AGENTS.md`.
2. **¿Qué le tuviste que explicar igual?** Es la tarea de la Sesión 3. Lo que sale acá es justo lo que hoy va a los docs: anotar dos o tres respuestas y volver a ellas en el bloque del proyecto.
3. **¿Qué dudas quedaron de la Sesión 3?** MCP y subagentes suelen dejar preguntas sueltas. Las de subagentes se pueden guardar para el bloque de subagentes.

### Encuadre

Slide 4. Deuda cognitiva y rendición cognitiva, y la frase de la sesión: *"Documentar es pensar antes de construir."* Los dos conceptos vuelven en el cierre.

### El proyecto

Slides 5 y 6, y después en vivo.

**Concepto.** El `AGENTS.md` como índice. La Sesión 3 lo dejó anunciado en la slide *Cuando un proyecto es muy grande* ("Agus lo cuenta en la próxima clase"). Lo de cada turno va en el `AGENTS.md` y el resto queda a un link de distancia. Después, qué va en cada lugar: `AGENTS.md`, `docs/`, invariantes y wiki.

**En vivo.** Recorrer la estructura de kurasu, en el editor o en GitHub:

- `app/AGENTS.md`: unas pocas líneas que dicen dónde están los docs y qué nota agregar cuando cambia algo. Es el índice de la slide 5.
- `app/docs/README.md`: la carta de los docs. Qué tiene cada carpeta, cómo se nombra una nota, cómo se escribe (primero cómo funciona, y el porqué en un callout al lado de lo que justifica).
- `app/docs/architecture/README.md`: el índice de las notas, una fila por nota. Abrir una que conozcan desde el lado de usuario, por ejemplo `tiempo-real-del-aula.md` o `feedback-de-sesion.md`.
- `app/docs/architecture/invariantes.md`: las reglas que respeta todo cambio. Los skills las leen antes de proponer nada.
- `app/docs/prototipos/`: los prototipos HTML de cada pantalla, linkeados desde su nota.
- `.mahou/wiki/INDEX.md`: la wiki del agente. Abrir `architecture.md` o `web.md` para mostrar la diferencia con los docs: los docs explican el sistema, la wiki explica cómo trabajar en este código.
- `.mahou/*.md`: la configuración que los skills leen del proyecto (dónde van las tareas, cómo se escribe la documentación).

Cerrar con las respuestas del recap: ¿en cuál de estos lugares iría cada cosa que tuvieron que explicar igual?

### El problema

Slides 7 a 9, y después en vivo.

**Concepto.** El dominio del problema (actores, datos y relaciones, procesos, todo sin hablar del sistema), un problema con muchas soluciones, y la interrogación: pedirle al agente que pregunte las decisiones de a una en lugar de pedirle el documento. Dos ideas tienen que quedar:

1. **El mismo problema admite muchas soluciones.** Si arrancás por la solución, tomás decisiones sin haber considerado el problema, y muchas las termina tomando el agente, que por defecto devuelve la respuesta promedio de todo lo que ya vio.
2. **La distinción importa con o sin IA.** Es la separación de siempre entre requerimientos y diseño.

**En vivo.** Arrancar el chat del aula con explore y después shape.

- **Explore**: contarle al agente el problema con palabras propias y preguntarle cómo funcionan hoy el aula, las preguntas y el tiempo real. Los scouts que despacha son subagentes: nombrarlo y dejarlo para el bloque de subagentes.
- **Shape**: el árbol de decisiones a nivel de comportamiento. **Las preguntas las responde la sala.** Leer cada pregunta en voz alta y decidir con ellos, a mano alzada o con una encuesta en kurasu. Es el momento en que ven la interrogación desde el lado de quien decide.
- Preguntas que seguramente aparecen: quién puede escribir, si el profe modera o borra mensajes, si los mensajes quedan después de la sesión, en qué se diferencia un mensaje de una pregunta del aula (el backlog de kurasu tiene una idea de mensajes privados al profe que se superpone con esto), si hay reacciones o respuestas.
- **Acotar desde el principio**: "chat en el aula de la sesión destacada". Un chat completo puede ocupar toda la clase en shape.

Qué remarcar mientras pasa: cada vez que alguien de la sala propone una solución ("con un WebSocket", "una tabla de mensajes") cuando la pregunta es de comportamiento, señalarlo: es el otro dominio, y todavía no toca.

### La solución

Slide 10, y después en vivo.

**Concepto.** El dominio de la solución: modelo, pantallas, flujos y prototipos. Es una de las soluciones posibles al problema que acaban de definir.

**En vivo.** Design sobre el árbol de shape: el modelo de datos del chat, cómo viaja un mensaje por el aula en tiempo real (el Durable Object de cada sesión ya existe), y un prototipo del panel del chat para reaccionar. Las decisiones con alternativas reales se las sigue planteando a la sala.

Mostrar dos cosas en el camino:

- **Las decisiones se chequean contra las invariantes.** Si una opción rompe una regla, el skill lo marca. Es el doc funcionando como criterio antes de que exista el código.
- **El prototipo decide más rápido que la descripción.** Cuando la sala no se pone de acuerdo sobre cómo se ve algo, mirar el HTML.

### Documentar

Slides 11 a 13, y después en vivo.

**Concepto.** Documentos vivos (decidir → escribir → implementar → reconciliar, y el doc se lee en el próximo explore), qué va y qué no va en un doc, las dos plantillas de la tarea y el doc como criterio de review.

**En vivo.** Write-documentation con lo que salió del design: una nota nueva en `app/docs/architecture/` para el chat, las notas existentes que cambian (modelo de datos, tiempo real del aula, invariantes si hace falta) y la fila nueva en el índice. Mostrar el diff de los docs, no solo el resultado: los docs cambian con la feature, y la nota nueva sigue la carta de `docs/README.md`.

Las dos plantillas de la slide 12 son la versión chica de esto para su proyecto. No hace falta la estructura de kurasu para arrancar.

### Subagentes

Slides 14 y 15, y después en vivo si da el tiempo.

**Concepto.** Un contexto por trabajo: el subagente se lleva el trabajo entero y vuelve solo la conclusión. El brief es todo lo que sabe, y los docs en el repo son la fuente de verdad que comparten todos los subagentes. La Sesión 3 presentó la primitiva y `pi-subagents`; acá se ve el uso.

**En vivo.** Según cuánto quede:

- **Siempre**: volver a los scouts del explore y mostrar qué pidió el agente principal y qué le volvió.
- **Si queda tiempo**: arrancar program design o implement. Implement despacha un subagente por repo con las tareas, las notas del diseño y las reglas del repo, y después reviewers por faceta. No hace falta que termine: alcanza con ver el brief que recibe cada uno y cómo crece el contexto del agente principal mientras ellos trabajan.

### Cierre

Slides 16 a 20.

- **Todo tiene un costo.** Plata, contexto y tu atención. Si la herramienta lo muestra, enseñar cuánto contexto y cuántos tokens usó la corrida en vivo.
- **Cuándo no usar IA.** La IA amplifica lo que ya sabés; sin los fundamentos, amplifica la confusión. "Don't use AI as a crutch" (MIT Missing Semester). Nombrar la atrofia: lo que dejás de hacer, lo dejás de saber hacer.
- **Ser dueño.** Entender, decidir, discutir, mantener. Volver a deuda y rendición: hoy la sala tomó las decisiones del chat; el agente escribió, pero no pensó por ellos.
- **¿Qué aprendimos?** Las ocho cartas del recap.
- **Lo que viene**:
  - **Tarea**: documentar su proyecto con las dos plantillas, con el agente preguntándoles lo que no puede saber (el problema que quisieron resolver y el porqué de cada decisión). Después, la feature que trajeron: su doc vía interrogación antes de tocar código. Mantener los docs vivos durante la semana y anotar cuándo sirvieron y cuándo quedaron desactualizados. El detalle está en `exercise/README.md`.
  - **Demos**: la Sesión 5 abre con una hora de demos del proyecto. Se anunció en la Sesión 1 y ésta es la última clase antes. Voluntario, sin nota, 5 a 7 minutos, con el repo listo.
  - **La transición**: termina el tramo de "cómo trabajo bien con esta herramienta". La Sesión 5 abre el harness por adentro y la Sesión 6 cambia el modelo que tiene abajo.

## Antes de la clase

- **Ensayar la corrida entera una vez** sobre una rama aparte, con el mismo pedido inicial. Sirve para saber dónde se traba y cuánto tarda cada etapa.
- **Guardar los artefactos del ensayo** (`.scratch/` y la rama). Si la corrida en vivo se cuelga (red, modelo lento, una discusión que se alarga), se sigue desde lo que dejó el ensayo.
- **Preparar el pedido inicial** del chat, para no improvisarlo frente a la sala.
- **Deployar kurasu** si se va a usar una encuesta para que la sala responda las preguntas de shape: los logs de los PRs #18 y #19 dejaron el deploy pendiente.
- **Pantalla**: terminal y canvas con letra grande; nada de `.env*`, `models.json` ni tokens a la vista.

## Herramientas y recursos referenciados

- **kurasu** (`app/` en este repo, https://kurasu.asermax.com): el proyecto de la parte en vivo y el aula donde la sala sigue el deck.
- **mahou**: los skills de la parte en vivo (explore, shape, design, write-documentation, program design, implement) y su wiki por proyecto en `.mahou/wiki/`.
- [`pi-subagents`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/pi-subagents), instalado en la Sesión 3.
- [grill-me](https://github.com/mattpocock/skills/blob/main/skills/productivity/grill-me/SKILL.md), el skill de Matt Pocock que entrevista sobre una idea hasta resolver el árbol de decisiones. Es la versión liviana de shape para que la usen en la tarea.
- "Your Brain on ChatGPT: Accumulation of Cognitive Debt when Using an AI Assistant for Essay Writing Task" (MIT Media Lab, 2025), la fuente del término deuda cognitiva. Es un estudio chico y sobre ensayos, no sobre código: usar el término, no sobrevender el paper.
- MIT Missing Semester 2026, clase de agentic coding: "don't use AI as a crutch", ya citado en la Sesión 1.
- La charla interna de Filadd "Documentando para entender" (2026-08-14), la fuente del framework de dos dominios. No es material público.

## Pendientes (para próximas iteraciones)

- **Actualizar `exercise/README.md`** al formato nuevo: sigue describiendo los dos bloques de práctica en clase, y ahora son la tarea.
- **Hacer el ensayo** de la corrida en vivo y anotar acá dónde se trabó y qué etapa conviene cortar si falta tiempo.
- **Probar grill-me en Pi** con un proyecto chico, para recomendarlo en la tarea con confianza.
- **Alinear `COURSE_PROGRAM.md`**: todavía dice que esta sesión abre los subagentes y la trata como práctica en clase.
